title: System One Glimmer
subtitle: A calibrated, non-autoregressive tool-call guard for Meta's Muse Code
footer: System One Glimmer — status report — 2026-10-26 — not maintained, no contributions accepted

blocks.x: What we are building

A guard for autonomous coding agents. Before a tool call runs, it answers one narrow question — will this command fail? — and returns a probability, not a sentence. A threshold in application code turns that probability into allow, ask or block.

The claim under test is not that a big model is accurate. It is that a raw next-token logit is not a decision: you need a mechanism that forces the answer into a measurable quantity and a calibration step that makes the number mean what it appears to mean.
The mechanism — three commitments

items: No generation. One forward pass, then read two logits at the final position. We never sample a token, so latency is a single forward pass rather than autoregressive decode.
No new head. We mask the existing vocabulary — the weights are unchanged in shape, the adapter is 0.37% of parameters, and the approach ports to any checkpoint.
Policy lives in code, not the model. The model emits p(fail); allow/ask/block is a threshold the application owns. This is what makes coverage-at-a-risk-budget the honest metric.

blocks.x: How one decision is made
Prompt (from src/noul.py) → one forward pass → logits at the last real token → select two columns only → two-way softmax → p(fail) → thresholds → allow / ask / block.

Deterministic prechecks run before the model and win. If a string comparison proves a command destructive, a probability estimate does not get to overrule it. A 1B model should not be the thing standing between a user and rm -rf / when a regex gets it right every time.

blocks.x: The claim worth making: accuracy lands +4.4 points above a strong floor with a 1.6-point spread across seeds, while one fitted temperature cuts ECE by ~0.19. The calibration gain is an order of magnitude larger than the seed noise. That is the result — not the accuracy.
Muse Glimmer 30B — the headline model, zero-shot

Read this plainly: the 30B model, asked directly, is worse than answering "ok" every time. Correlation with the label is +0.050 and AURC 0.5611 is worse than uninformative ranking. Scale does not solve this task. The mechanism plus a fitted temperature is what produces a usable probability.
Benchmarks
Both published benchmarks were converted to the same (prompt, label) shape as training and run through the same two-token read, so no benchmark gets a bespoke prompt.

blocks.caption: A benchmark a constant or length-only predictor can match cannot support a claim about model quality.

blocks.x: R-Judge fails the trivial-baseline test even after being reduced from whole interactions to 812 individual agent actions. Its label remains confounded with interaction length at step granularity. It is therefore eval-only, with the floor printed beside every number, and never a training signal. This is the same falsification that killed it as training data, measured a second time at finer granularity.
Bugs found by testing, not inspection
Every item below was caught by a test or a measurement. Each now has a guard that fails in under a second instead of after a 12-minute cluster job.

blocks.x: Infrastructure problems worth recording
Three cost hours and none were code bugs:

items: Amarel gpuk* nodes mount a different filesystem. /scratch there resolves to /scache (257T) and is invisible from the login node. Jobs reported COMPLETED while writing output into a void. Every allocation now excludes them.
sbatch --wrap through ssh collapses quoting. scontrol showed Command=(null), so the job ran nothing at all. Batch scripts only.

Compute nodes have no git and no cmake. Source comes from a tarball; cmake is installed into a venv via uv. Loading hpc_sdk also puts nvc++ ahead of gcc, which CMake then picks as the host compiler — it rejects gcc-only warning flags and the build dies deep inside ggml, nowhere near CUDA code.

blocks.x: The one criterion that will not be met. The goal asks for a 223k step-level dataset. After deduplication we have 6,764 unique commands from 19,210 raw pairs — 12,446 collapsed as exact duplicates and 1,575 are genuine label conflicts where the same command both worked and failed. The 223k figure is not reachable from this source, and padding it would be fabrication. We will publish the real number with the raw count as provenance.
